subject: forensic-medicine
title: Inquest, courts and medical evidence

steps.tx: An **inquest** is an inquiry into the cause and manner of an unnatural, sudden or suspicious death. In India it is carried out by a police officer under Section 174 of the CrPC, or by a magistrate under Section 176. The police inquest is the most common type. Its purpose is to establish identity and cause of death, not to decide guilt.

steps.tx: Magistrate inquest is mandatory for deaths in prison, police custody or during police firing, dowry deaths within **7 years of marriage**, exhumation, and deaths in psychiatric hospitals. A police inquest covers suicide, homicide, accident and deaths raising suspicion of another person's offence. Remember that exhumation always needs a magistrate's order.

steps.tx: **Dowry death** under Section 304B IPC applies when a woman dies from bodily injury, burns or other causes in suspicious circumstances within **7 years of marriage**, and soon before death she faced harassment or cruelty over dowry. Punishment is imprisonment of not less than 10 years, extendable to life. Cruelty by husband or relatives under Section 498A carries up to 3 years and fine.

steps.tx: Courts have set sentencing limits. A **Chief Judicial Magistrate** may impose up to 7 years imprisonment, a first class magistrate up to 3 years or a fine of 10,000 rupees, and a second class magistrate up to 1 year or 5000 rupees, under Section 29 CrPC. The **Assistant Sessions Court** can give up to 10 years. The **Sessions Court** can award any sentence, including death, which must be confirmed by the High Court.

steps.tx: Medical evidence is documentary or oral. **Oral evidence** is preferred because it allows **cross examination**. Exceptions where a document suffices include a **dying declaration**, a doctor's evidence recorded in a lower court, chemical examiner reports, and hospital records. A **subpoena** is the legal summons compelling a witness to attend court.
